Only partly. Sending the token as the WebSocket subprotocol keeps it out of the request line, so a URL-based access log won't capture it. It is not fully safe from logging, because the token still travels in the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` request header. Any ingress log that captures headers, proxy trace or debug logging can pick it up there. Issue #150 says the documented claim of avoiding log exposure was 'only half true'.

The original design echoed the token back in the 101 response headers and held it on the socket object. That made it visible to header-capturing logs and to a debug `console.log(ws)`. The fix in #150 changed this. The client now offers `hal.v1, <token>` and the server answers only the marker `hal.v1`. The token stays out of the response headers and off the socket's `protocol` property. HAL Engine 0.3.0 and later behave this way.

The remaining request-header exposure means operators must configure log redaction for that header. The issue also requires that no offered subprotocol value be written to any log, including in the close handler.

The token must also fit the HTTP-token character set, so padded base64 tokens can't use this carrier.

judgements.reason: The answer says it is not fully safe, explains that the server echoed the token into the 101 response headers where logs could capture it, and describes the fix: the client offers hal.v1 then the token, and the server selects the marker.
